content: Ovalbumin is the predominant protein present in egg white, accounting for approximately 60-65% of the total protein content. It is classified as a member of the serpin superfamily of proteins. However, unlike most serpins, ovalbumin does not possess the ability to inhibit proteases. The precise biological function of ovalbumin remains unclear, but it is hypothesized to serve as a storage protein. Ovalbumin plays a significant role in various research domains. It is widely utilized in general studies of protein structure and properties due to its availability in large quantities. In the study of serpin structure and function, ovalbumin is particularly valuable because its inability to inhibit proteases allows researchers to compare its structure with inhibitory serpins, thereby identifying the structural features necessary for protease inhibition. In proteomics, chicken egg ovalbumin is frequently employed as a molecular weight marker for calibrating electrophoresis gels. Additionally, in immunology, ovalbumin is commonly used to induce allergic reactions in experimental subjects for research purposes. The structure of chicken ovalbumin consists of 385 amino acids, with a relative molecular mass of 45 kDa. It is a glycoprotein containing four glycosylation sites. Despite lacking an N-terminal leader sequence, ovalbumin is secreted from the cell. From a medicinal perspective, ovalbumin has applications in cases of suspected heavy metal poisoning, such as iron toxicity. Ovalbumin has the ability to chelate heavy metals, binding the metal ions within the sulfhydryl bonds of the protein. This chelation process prevents the absorption of the metals into the gastrointestinal tract, thereby mitigating the risk of poisoning.
